Doob’s Maximal Inequality: Making the “Maximum” Controllable¶

Roadmap¶

  1. Maximal process: $M_n^*=\max_{k\le n} M_k$ and $\sup_{t\le T} M_t$
  2. Doob’s first (weak-type) inequality: tail control via a stopping time
  3. Doob’s $L^p$ inequality: strong $L^p$ control + the sharp constant $p/(p-1)$
  4. Continuous time: how discretisation + right-continuity lifts discrete inequalities to $[0,T]$
  5. Why this matters: convergence + the Itô integral construction as a process
  6. Monte Carlo “sanity checks”: random walk / exponential martingale
  7. Advanced experiment: Doob $L^2$ as the engine behind “process-level” convergence of Itô sums

1. The object: maximal processes¶

Discrete time¶

Given a (nonnegative) submartingale $(M_n)_{n\ge 0}$, define the maximal sequence

$$M_n^*(\omega):=\max_{0\le k\le n} M_k(\omega).$$

Continuous time¶

Given an adapted process $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, define the running supremum

$$M_T^*(\omega):=\sup_{0\le t\le T} M_t(\omega).$$

The philosophical move: turn “the path” into one statistic.

Doob’s inequalities say: that statistic is not wild; it is measurable and controllable.

Nerd note: “maximal inequality” is martingale-world’s version of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator.

2. Doob’s maximal inequality (weak-type / tail control)¶

Discrete time: the basic inequality¶

Let $(M_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a nonnegative submartingale. For any $\alpha>0$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$\alpha\,\mathbb P(M_n^*\ge \alpha) \le \mathbb E\left(M_n\,\mathbf 1_{\{M_n^*\ge \alpha\}}\right) \le \mathbb E(M_n)$$

In particular,

$$\mathbb P(M_n^*\ge \alpha) \le \frac{\mathbb E(M_n)}{\alpha}$$

Proof skeleton (stopping time view)¶

Define the first passage time

$$\tau := \min\{k\le n: M_k\ge \alpha\} \quad(\text{with } \tau=\infty \text{ if never reached})$$

Then the key identity is

$$\{M_n^*\ge \alpha\}=\{\tau\le n\}$$

Now observe two facts:

  1. On $\{\tau\le n\}$, we have $M_{\tau}\ge \alpha$, hence $M_{\tau\wedge n}\ge \alpha\,\mathbf 1_{\{\tau\le n\}}$.
  2. Because $M$ is a submartingale, optional sampling gives $\mathbb E[M_{\tau\wedge n}] \le \mathbb E[M_n]$.

Combine them:

$$\alpha\,\mathbb P(M_n^*\ge \alpha) = \alpha\,\mathbb P(\tau\le n) \le \mathbb E[M_{\tau\wedge n}] \le \mathbb E[M_n]$$

What if $M$ is a martingale that can change sign?¶

Apply the inequality to the submartingale $|M_n|$ (convexity / Jensen gives that $|M_n|$ is a submartingale).

3. Doob’s $L^p$ inequality (stronger control)¶

For $1<p<\infty$ and a martingale (or nonnegative submartingale),

$$\|M_n^*\|_p \le \frac{p}{p-1}\|M_n\|_p, \qquad \text{and in continuous time } \Big\|\sup_{t\le T}M_t\Big\|_p\le \frac{p}{p-1}\|M_T\|_p.$$

How the proof works (tail $\to$ moment)¶

The key “layer-cake” identity is:

$$\|X\|_p^p = \mathbb E[X^p] = p\int_0^\infty \lambda^{p-1}\,\mathbb P(X>\lambda)\,d\lambda \quad\text{for }X\ge 0.$$

Now plug in the weak-type inequality for $X=M_n^*$ and choose $Y=M_n$:

$$\lambda\,\mathbb P(M_n^*>\lambda) \le \mathbb E\left(M_n\mathbf 1_{\{M_n^*>\lambda\}}\right).$$

Integrate against $p\lambda^{p-2}\,d\lambda$, swap integrals (Fubini), and finish with Hölder’s inequality.

About the constant¶

A common intermediate bound produces $2p/(p-1)$, but with a sharper argument one gets the optimal $p/(p-1)$. We’ll compare empirically to $p/(p-1)$ below.

4. Continuous time: why discretisation is not cheating¶

For continuous (right-continuous is enough) submartingales, Doob’s inequalities on $[0,T]$ can be obtained by:

  1. Sample on a grid: $t_k = kT/2^n$. Consider the discrete sequence $M_{t_k}$.
  2. Apply discrete-time Doob to the sampled process.
  3. Let the grid get finer and pass to the limit using:
  • monotone convergence for the supremum over an increasing grid,
  • right-continuity to identify $\sup_{t\le T}$ with the limit over grids.

5. Why we care (the non-hyped version)¶

Doob’s inequalities are the workhorses for statements like:

  • Convergence: if a martingale is bounded in $L^p$ (especially $p>1$), its maximal process is also controlled in $L^p$.
  • Process-level limits: in a standard construction of the Itô integral as a process $t\mapsto \int_0^t f\,dB$, the key estimate is of the form

$$\mathbb P\Big(\sup_{t\le T}|X_t^{(n)}-X_t^{(m)}|>\varepsilon\Big) \lesssim \varepsilon^{-2} \mathbb E|X_T^{(n)}-X_T^{(m)}|^2,$$

i.e., “terminal $L^2$ control $\Rightarrow$ uniform-in-time control”.

We’ll build a simulation that mirrors this argument in Section 7. (Note: The roadmap says Section 7 for the advanced experiment, so I've adjusted the section number reference here slightly to match your roadmap!)

6. Visual experiment A — sample paths and the running maximum¶

We start with a simple martingale: the symmetric random walk $S_n$. Since $|S_n|$ is a nonnegative submartingale, Doob applies to $M_n:=|S_n|$.

We plot both $M_n$ and its running maximum $M_n^*$.

Figure 1. Nonnegative submartingale example: absolute random walk paths.

Figure 2. Running maximum turns each path into a monotone (increasing) process.

7. Visual experiment B — checking the tail bound¶

We compare the empirical estimate of $\mathbb P(M_n^*\ge \alpha)$ with the Doob bound $\mathbb E(M_n)/\alpha$.

The inequality is typically loose (it must hold for all nonnegative submartingales).

Figure 3. Empirical tail probability of the running maximum versus the Doob upper bound. Doob controls the event 'the maximum is large' via only the terminal expectation E(M_n).

8. Visual experiment C — checking the $L^p$ inequality¶

We estimate the ratio $$ R_p := \frac{\|M_n^*\|_p}{\|M_n\|_p} $$

and compare it to the theoretical constant $\frac{p}{p-1}$.

Figure 4. Empirical L^p ratio compared to the theoretical constant p/(p−1). Doob predicts the ratio stays below p/(p−1).

9. Optional: a positive exponential martingale example¶

Define $$ M_n=\exp(\theta S_n - n\log\cosh(\theta)), $$

a classic positive martingale for the symmetric random walk. We repeat the ratio experiment.

10. Advanced visual experiment — Doob $L^2$ drives “process-level” convergence (Itô sums)¶

This is the move that shows up when you construct the Itô integral as a process.

Setup¶

  • Simulate Brownian motion $B_t$ on a fine grid.
  • Fix a deterministic integrand $f(t)$ (bounded, nice).
  • Build two Itô-sum approximations $I_t^{(N_1)}$ and $I_t^{(N_2)}$ using partitions of different sizes.
  • Look at the difference process $\Delta_t := I_t^{(N_1)} - I_t^{(N_2)}$.

Because each approximation is a martingale in $t$, the difference $\Delta_t$ is also a martingale.

Doob $L^2$ predicts

$$\mathbb P\Big(\sup_{t\le T}|\Delta_t|>\varepsilon\Big) \le \frac{\mathbb E|\Delta_T|^2}{\varepsilon^2}.$$

We’ll estimate both sides by Monte Carlo.

Figure 5. The Doob $L^2$ bound is conservative but captures the right logic: if the terminal $L^2$ error is small, large uniform-in-time deviations become unlikely.

Figure 6. Differences of two Itô-sum approximations behave like a (small) martingale in time.
